title_en: American President Lines Ltd. v. Feida Electric Appliance Factory, Feili Company, and Great Wall Company — retrial of dispute over delivery of goods without bills of lading

full_text_en:
American President Lines Ltd. v. Feida Electric Appliance Factory, Phillips Co., and Great Wall Company — Retrial of a Dispute over Delivery of Goods Without Original Bills of Lading

Applicant for Retrial (Original Appellant and Defendant at First Instance): American President Lines Ltd. Domicile: Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Legal Representative: David L. Atarling
Agent ad litem: Jin Qingjun, Zhang Hengshun, lawyers of Shenzhen Xinda Law Firm, Guangdong Province.

Original Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Wanbao Group Guangzhou Feida Electric Appliance Factory. Domicile: Jiangyan Road, Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province.
Legal Representative: Deng Shaoyi, Factory Director.

Original Appellee (Third Party at First Instance): China Great Wall Industry Guangzhou Company. Domicile: Guangyuan West Road, Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province.
Legal Representative: Gong Lixing, General Manager of the Company.

Original Appellee (Third Party at First Instance): Phillips (Guangzhou) Industrial Co., Ltd. (dissolved).

The original appellant, American President Lines Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "APL"), dissatisfied with the civil judgment of second instance rendered by the Guangdong High People's Court in the case concerning a dispute over delivery of goods without original bills of lading with the original appellees, Wanbao Group Guangzhou Feida Electric Appliance Factory (hereinafter referred to as "Feida Factory"), Phillips (Guangzhou) Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Phillips Company"), and China Great Wall Industry Guangzhou Company (hereinafter referred to as "Great Wall Company"), applied to the Supreme People's Court of the People's Republic of China for a retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled: to bring this case up for trial and to suspend the execution of the judgment of the original instance during the retrial period. During the period of the trial brought up, Phillips Company, due to reasons such as failure to undergo annual inspection, long-term business cessation, and the whereabouts of the company and its legal representative being unknown, had been dissolved by the Guangzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce on December 30, 1997. No company declared that it would assume the creditor's rights and debts of Phillips Company. Accordingly, the Supreme People's Court, in accordance with the law, revoked Phillips Company's status as a party in this case.

The original judgment found: On July 29, 1993, the appellee Feida Factory and GB Lighting Supplier (Singapore) (hereinafter referred to as "GB Lighting") entered into an agreement by facsimile, stipulating: Feida Factory would export a batch of lighting fixtures to GB Lighting; after Feida Factory shipped the goods, it would send the bill of lading by facsimile; GB Lighting must remit the full amount of the payment within three days; after Feida Factory received a copy of the remittance advice, it would then deliver the original bill of lading to GB Lighting; any act of taking delivery of goods in violation of the law would be treated as fraud.

After the agreement was signed, the appellee Feida Factory, on August 14, 1993, instructed the appellee Great Wall Company to handle the export procedures for 910 cases of lighting fixtures and transformers, and on August 21, instructed Guangzhou Foreign Enterprise Materials Import and Export Company to handle the export procedures for 783 cases of lighting fixtures. After accepting the instruction, Guangzhou Foreign Enterprise Materials Import and Export Company delegated it to its subordinate, the appellee Phillips Company, for execution. Great Wall Company and Phillips Company, respectively, as shippers at Huangpu Port, loaded two containers containing Feida Factory's goods onto the vessels "EAGLEWAVE V.002" and "EAGLE COMET V.112" owned by the appellant APL, and entrusted it with the carriage. APL accordingly issued to Great Wall Company and Phillips Company straight bills of lading in a set of three, numbered APLU023158043 and APLU023157949, respectively. Both bills of lading recorded: the carrier was APL, the consignee was GB Lighting, the port of loading was Huangpu, the port of discharge was Singapore, and freight was prepaid. The Export Goods Customs Declaration Form provided by Huangpu Customs confirmed that the trade term for the goods under both bills of lading was FOB, and the value of the goods was USD 58,994.148 and USD 39,669, respectively.

After the aforementioned goods arrived at the port of destination, Singapore, the buyer GB Lighting did not pay the appellee Feida Factory in accordance with the agreement, but instead, without obtaining the original bills of lading, wrote to the appellant APL on September 16 and September 17, 1993, respectively, requesting APL to deliver the two lots of goods to the land carrier designated by it, YUNG XIE Transport (Private) Ltd., vehicle number 13445880000C, and guaranteed to assume any consequences that might arise therefrom. The Port Authority of Singapore confirmed that these two lots of goods had been delivered and released on September 16 and 17, 1993, respectively.

The paramount clauses on the reverse side of the bills of lading for both lots of goods stipulated: "The receipt, custody, carriage, and delivery of the goods are governed by the terms of the contract of carriage evidenced by this bill of lading, including... (3) The provisions of the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1936, or the law of a country where the Hague Rules, as amended by the Brussels Convention of 1924, are in force, as determined by a court of competent jurisdiction for disputes arising from the contract of carriage."

The appellee Feida Factory, holding the full set of original bills of lading for the above two lots of goods, filed a lawsuit with the Guangzhou Maritime Court on the grounds that the appellant APL delivered the goods without the original bills of lading. The appellees Great Wall Company and Phillips Company simultaneously applied to participate in the lawsuit as third parties and expressed support for Feida Factory's claims. After the Guangzhou Maritime Court accepted the case in accordance with the law, it ruled to allow Great Wall Company and Phillips Company to participate in the lawsuit as third parties. APL did not raise any objection to jurisdiction and responded to the lawsuit.

After trial, the Guangzhou Maritime Court, in accordance with Article 71 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "Maritime Code"), Articles 106 and 117 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "General Principles of Civil Law"), and international customs, rendered a judgment: APL was to compensate Feida Factory for the loss of goods amounting to USD 98,666.148 and interest. The interest was to be calculated from September 17, 1993, until the effective date of the judgment, at the US dollar loan interest rate for working capital of the People's Bank of China during the same period.

Dissatisfied with the first instance judgment of the Guangzhou Maritime Court, APL appealed to the Guangdong High People's Court. The reasons were: (1) According to the agreement in the contract of carriage between the parties, this case should be governed by US law or Singapore law. The practice of delivering goods only against surrender of original bills of lading is, in international custom, aimed at negotiable bills of lading which serve as documents of title. Chinese law explicitly requires that the carrier can only deliver the goods under a straight bill of lading to the consignee named therein. This is the carrier's undertaking when issuing a straight bill of lading, irrespective of how the original bill of lading is held. (2) The appellee did not notify APL to suspend delivery of the goods to the consignee named in the straight bill of lading, allowing the loss to occur, and should bear the consequences. The judgment ordering APL to compensate Feida Factory for the loss of USD 98,666.148 and interest was unfounded. The first instance judgment erred in the application of law and should be corrected.

The Guangdong High People's Court held in its final instance:

This case is a foreign-related economic dispute. The appellee Feida Factory filed an action in tort on the grounds that APL's delivery of goods without original bills of lading infringed upon its ownership. The rights and obligations between the parties should be governed by the norms of tort law, not by the original contract of carriage between them. Article 146 of the General Principles of Civil Law provides: "Compensation for damages arising from a tort shall be governed by the law of the place where the tort was committed." Article 187 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China stipulates: "The law of the place where a tort is committed includes the law of the place where the tortious act is carried out and the law of the place where the result of the tort occurs. If the two are inconsistent, the people's court may choose to apply one of them." In this case, the place of delivery of the goods was Singapore, and the place where the tortious act was carried out was Singapore; Feida Factory held the original bills of lading, and the act of delivering goods without original bills of lading infringed upon its ownership of the goods, so the place where the result of the tort occurred was China. Since the place where the tortious act was carried out and the place where the result occurred were inconsistent, the people's court could choose the applicable law. As the place where the result of the tort occurred was China, the plaintiff's domicile, the place where the bills of lading were issued, etc., were also within China, this case had a closer connection with Chinese law. Moreover, after Feida Factory filed the lawsuit with the Guangzhou Maritime Court, the appellant APL did not raise any objection to jurisdiction and responded to the lawsuit. Therefore, it was not improper for the Guangzhou Maritime Court to exercise jurisdiction over this case and choose to apply Chinese law. APL's appeal argument that US law or Singapore law should be applied to this case lacked reason and basis and was not adopted.

Article 71 of the Maritime Code provides: "A bill of lading is a document which serves as evidence of the contract of carriage of goods by sea and the taking over or loading of the goods by the carrier, and based on which the carrier undertakes to deliver the goods. A clause in the bill of lading stating that the goods are to be delivered to a named person, or to order, or to the holder of the bill of lading, constitutes an undertaking by the carrier to deliver the goods accordingly." There is no dispute between the parties that the appellee Feida Factory is the shipper and owner of the goods involved in this case. From the fact that Feida Factory still holds the original bills of lading, it can be seen that the bills of lading have not been transferred, which should be regarded as the goods not having been delivered and the title to the goods not having passed to the buyer under the sales contract. Feida Factory is in fact still the owner of the goods in this case. The appellant APL, without obtaining the consent of the shipper Feida Factory and without collecting the original bills of lading, delivered the goods to a person who was not the holder of the original bills of lading, violating the provision of the Maritime Code that the carrier should deliver the goods against surrender of original bills of lading, and infringing upon Feida Factory's ownership of the goods. Feida Factory has the right to file an action in tort with the court. APL shall bear full responsibility for delivering the goods to a person not holding the original bills of lading and compensate Feida Factory for the losses suffered thereby. Calculated based on the FOB price confirmed by the customs, the total loss was USD 98,666.148.

The appellant APL argued that the delivery of goods only against surrender of original bills of lading as an international custom is only applicable to negotiable bills of lading which serve as documents of title. APL did not provide corresponding evidence for this argument, so it was not supported. Furthermore, the Maritime Code already contains provisions regarding the carrier's delivery of goods against original bills of lading, so there is no need to consider the application of international custom in this case.

Article 71 of the Maritime Code only provides that a bill of lading is a document based on which the carrier undertakes to deliver the goods, and does not distinguish between straight bills of lading and negotiable bills of lading. Therefore, this article should be interpreted to mean that, regardless of whether the bill of lading is a straight bill of lading or a negotiable one, the carrier has the obligation to deliver the goods against the original bill of lading. The appellant APL's appeal argument that Chinese law explicitly requires the carrier to only deliver the goods under a straight bill of lading to the consignee named therein, and that this is the carrier's undertaking when issuing a straight bill of lading, irrespective of how the original bill of lading is held, is a misinterpretation of Article 71 of the Maritime Code by APL.

The fact that the appellee Feida Factory did not notify the appellant APL to suspend delivery of the goods to the consignee named in the straight bill of lading does not relieve the carrier of its obligation to deliver the goods against original bills of lading, nor does it imply that Feida Factory allowed the loss to occur. APL's appeal argument that Feida Factory failed to exercise its rights and allowed the loss to occur, and should bear the consequences, is untenable.

The first instance judgment had clear findings of fact, conclusive evidence, correct application of law, proper procedures, and appropriate results, so it should be upheld. Accordingly, the Guangdong High People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered a judgment: the appeal was dismissed and the original judgment was affirmed.

Dissatisfied, APL applied to the Supreme People's Court for a retrial and also requested the suspension of the execution of the final judgment of the Guangdong High People's Court. The reasons were: (1) A bill of lading is one of the written forms of a contract of carriage of goods by sea. The delivery of goods under a bill of lading is the performance of the contract of carriage of goods by sea. This case is purely a dispute over a contract of carriage of goods by sea. The focus of the dispute between the parties is whether the carrier, without seeing the original straight bill of lading, delivering the goods under the bill of lading to the consignee named therein complies with the terms of the contract of carriage of goods by sea. This differs from a tort dispute where, without contractual agreement, the carrier delivers goods without seeing the original bill of lading, infringing upon the property rights of the cargo owner. The original judgment erred in finding that the carrier's delivery of goods without the original straight bill of lading in this case was an action in tort, not a dispute over a contract of carriage of goods by sea. (2) The paramount clause of the straight bill of lading involved in this case explicitly states that disputes arising from this bill of lading shall be governed by the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936 or the Hague Rules. This choice of law is a legally valid choice by the parties and is binding on all parties. The original judgment disregarded the parties' choice of law and relevant international customs, treating the relatively independent relationship under maritime law as a general civil tort relationship, resulting in an error in the application of law. (3) As the carrier, the appellant had no fault in delivering the goods to the named consignee under the straight bill of lading. After the appellee sent the bill of lading by fax to GB Lighting and did not receive payment from GB Lighting on time, it failed to exercise its right under the law to notify the carrier to stop delivering the goods to GB Lighting, allowing GB Lighting to smoothly and legally take delivery of the goods in Singapore. The appellee has no right to claim compensation from the appellant, who was without fault.

Feida Factory filed a written defense with the following reasons: (1) This case is a dispute over an international contract of carriage of goods by sea and should be governed by the relevant laws on carriage of goods by sea. The key issue to be resolved is whether the carrier's delivery of goods without original bills of lading is legal. (2) The reverse side clause of the bill of lading in this case stipulated the application of the Hague Rules or the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936. This was a voluntary agreement between the parties and is legally valid. However, this agreement did not specify whether the Hague Rules or the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936 should be applied selectively or concurrently; moreover, neither of these laws provides for or clearly stipulates whether the carrier's delivery of goods against a copy of the bill of lading is legal, thereby affecting the allocation of rights and obligations between the parties. (3) The appellant's issuance of an anti-dated bill of lading constitutes an act of fraud and a fundamental breach of contract, and it is precluded from invoking the choice of law clause in the bill of lading to raise a defense. In this situation, applying Chinese law and relevant international shipping customs becomes the only option. (4) A bill of lading is a document of title, evidence of the contract of carriage by sea, and a document based on which the carrier promises to deliver the goods. Chinese law explicitly provides that the carrier has the obligation to deliver the goods against original bills of lading. According to shipping practice, the carrier's delivery of goods against original bills of lading is an implied undertaking, and this undertaking applies equally to straight bills of lading. Therefore, the appellant must bear responsibility for delivering goods without original bills of lading. (5) While the original judgment may have certain deficiencies, this does not negate the fact that the appellant is responsible for the losses caused to the appellee by delivering goods without original bills of lading.

The appellee Great Wall Company did not submit a defense.

The Supreme People's Court, upon bringing the case up for trial, ascertained: The original appellant APL and the original appellee Feida Factory had no dispute regarding the basic facts found in the original trial. Although the original third parties Great Wall Company and Phillips Company applied and were permitted by the court of first instance to participate in the lawsuit, they both acknowledged that they had no interest whatsoever in the goods under the bills of lading in this case and participated in the lawsuit solely to support Feida Factory's claims against APL.

The Supreme People's Court, after trial, held:

The focus of the dispute between the parties is the applicable law to this case and whether the carrier should deliver the goods to the named consignee who does not hold the original straight bill of lading.

Both parties have no objection that this case is a dispute over the delivery of goods without original bills of lading under an international contract of carriage of goods by sea, and this should be confirmed. Article 269 of the Maritime Code provides: "The parties to a contract may choose the law applicable to the contract, unless otherwise provided by law. If the parties to a contract have not chosen the applicable law, the law of the country having the closest connection with the contract shall apply." The bills of lading in this case were voluntarily chosen for use by the parties, and the paramount clause explicitly stipulated the application of the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936 or the Hague Rules. This choice of law reflects the true intention of the parties, does not violate the public interest of the People's Republic of China, is legally valid, and should be respected. However, since Article 1 of the Hague Rules provides that the Rules apply only to contracts of carriage covered by a document of title, and the bills of lading in this case are non-negotiable straight bills of lading which do not have the effect of a document of title, and furthermore, the Hague Rules do not provide for how the carrier should deliver goods under a straight bill of lading, the dispute over the contract of carriage of goods by sea in this case cannot be governed by the Hague Rules, but only by the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936. Section 3(4) of the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936 provides that nothing in this Act shall be construed as repealing or limiting the application of the US Federal Bills of Lading Act. In fact, when applying the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936 to confirm the legal relationship involving bills of lading, it is only by applying the related US Federal Bills of Lading Act together that the rights and obligations of the parties in the contract of carriage of goods by sea evidenced by the bill of lading can be accurately and consistently determined. Therefore, this case should be governed by the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936 and the US Federal Bills of Lading Act. The original appellee Feida Factory's argument in its defense that Chinese law should apply to this case does not comply with the parties' agreement in the contract and is not supported. The original court's determination that this case was a tort dispute and its application of Chinese law on the ground that the place where the result of the tort occurred was China do not conform to the facts of this case and constitute an error in the application of law, which should be corrected.

Although the shippers named on the bills of lading in this case are the original appellees Great Wall Company and Phillips Company, Great Wall Company and Phillips Company were merely export agents of the original appellee Feida Factory. All parties acknowledge that Feida Factory is the actual shipper of the goods in question. Feida Factory, as the shipper, legally holds the bills of lading issued by the original appellant APL. Therefore, the international contract of carriage of goods by sea between Feida Factory and APL, as evidenced by the bills of lading, is legally valid.

A straight bill of lading differs from a negotiable bill of lading. A straight bill of lading is a non-negotiable transport document and does not have the effect of a document of title, whereas a negotiable bill of lading is transferable and has the effect of a document of title. According to the provisions of the US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of 1936 and Sections 2 and 9(b) of the US Federal Bills of Lading Act, the carrier is entitled to deliver the goods to the consignee named by the shipper in the straight bill of lading. When delivering goods to the named consignee under a straight bill of lading, the carrier is not obligated to require the named consignee to present or surrender the straight bill of lading. The original appellant APL, as the carrier, delivered the goods to the named consignee GB Lighting in accordance with the terms of the straight bill of lading, or, at GB Lighting's request, delivered the goods to the land carrier designated by GB Lighting. This act of delivery complied with the provisions of the aforementioned US law and constituted a proper performance of the obligation to deliver the goods under the contract of carriage of goods by sea. APL was not at fault. APL's application for retrial is well-founded and should be supported.

Before the goods were delivered at the port of destination, the original appellee Feida Factory did not notify the original appellant APL, as the carrier, to cease delivery of the goods to the consignee named in the straight bill of lading. The consequences arising therefrom shall be borne by Feida Factory itself. Feida Factory's loss from not receiving payment is a risk inherent in its trade with GB Lighting and is unrelated to APL. The original judgment's finding that APL failed to properly perform its obligation to deliver the goods against original bills of lading was improper, and its decision ordering APL to compensate Feida Factory for the loss of the goods was erroneous and should be corrected.

The Appellee at First Instance, Feida Factory, argued in its defense that the Appellant at First Instance, Meilun Company, had issued an advance bill of lading, but did not submit relevant evidence to support this claim. Moreover, whether the bill of lading in question was an advance bill of lading was unrelated to Feida Factory’s original claims, and thus this Court does not address the issue.

In summary, the Supreme People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, item (2) and Article 184 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rendered the following judgment on June 25, 2002:

1. Set aside the civil judgment of the second instance rendered by the Guangdong High People's Court.

2. Set aside the civil judgment of the first instance rendered by the Guangzhou Maritime Court.

3. Dismiss all claims of the Appellee at First Instance, Feida Factory, against the Appellant at First Instance, Meilun Company.

The litigation costs for the first instance, RMB 41,490, and for the second instance, RMB 41,490, shall be borne by the Appellee at First Instance, Feida Factory.

This judgment is final.
